title: The Quiet Well
premise: Sebastian Vane hosts a small-town overnight radio show, and one week after the Hollow Creek flood, the calls start coming from listeners who drowned. When his own sleep-recording app captures a second voice answering questions he never asked aloud, he learns the dead are not haunting him — they are recruiting him. The voice belongs to something beneath the old Vane family well, something fed in 1974 when Sebastian's grandfather traded the town's missing children for the town's prosperity. To free himself and the trapped callers, Sebastian must return what was taken: not an object, but the truth of a confession that was buried along with them. In the end he broadcasts the confession live, lets the well take him as payment, and dies on air — though the final chapter suggests his voice is still answering call-ins, patient and kind.
about_author: Juniper Whitlock is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent six years answering phones for insomniacs, conspiracy theorists, and the recently bereaved. She writes horror about small towns, dead frequencies, and the things people confess to strangers at 3 a.m.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. A week after the Hollow Creek flood, Sebastian's overnight show receives a call from Marla Tetch — who drowned last Tuesday. He keeps her on the line until dawn, telling himself it's a prank, then finds her flooded basement address written in his own handwriting. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professional calm; the first crack in his rational world.

chapters.title: The Counting House
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Sebastian reveals his compulsions to the reader: doors counted, lights kept on, a ritual inherited from his grandfather Aldous. Another dead caller, a boy named Danny, asks him a question no caller could know: 'Why do you count, Seb?' Emotional beat: isolation deepening; the horror turns intimate, aimed at his private rituals.

chapters.title: Sleep Study
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Reviewing his sleep-recording app for evidence of stress-talking, Sebastian hears a second voice — low, wet, unhurried — answering questions in his pauses. It knows his grandfather's name. He plays the clip until 4 a.m., then realizes the voice has begun asking its own questions. Emotional beat: vertigo; the boundary between listener and host collapses.

chapters.title: What Aldous Built
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian, with flashback interludes from Aldous Vane, 1974. At the county archive Sebastian finds the flood of '74 erased from every record, but a librarian remembers: three children went into the Vane well, and the town got a new mill, new money, new silence. Emotional beat: complicity; Sebastian feels the family debt settle onto his shoulders like silt.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. The dead callers multiply, each one kinder than the last, each steering him toward the well site. Danny admits they aren't haunting him — they're using him as a door, because the thing below needs a Vane to open it. Emotional beat: betrayal and tenderness tangled; even the dead lie to survive.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV the voice beneath the well. For one chapter the narrative drowns: the entity recounts 1974 from below — the children's arrival, Aldous's bargain, fifty years of listening upward through soil and pipe. It explains why it answers Sebastian's sleeping questions: it is lonely, and loneliness is how it feeds. Emotional beat: horrifying sympathy; the monster wants belonging too.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. The station becomes a trap — exits lead back to Studio B, the door count climbs past what exists. The entity offers a bargain: keep broadcasting the dead forever, beloved and safe, or come down and end it. Sebastian realizes his rituals were never comfort; they were maintenance, keeping the seal Aldous installed. Emotional beat: claustrophobic temptation; safety offered at the price of everyone else.

chapters.title: Loyalty
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. His oldest friend Ruth, the show's engineer, discovers the recordings and begs him to walk away — the town knew in '74, she says, and the town chose silence; let it stay chosen. Sebastian must choose between protecting the living who enabled the crime and freeing the children who paid for it. Emotional beat: loyalty versus truth made explicit; friendship strained to breaking.

chapters.title: Open Line
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Climax. Sebastian takes the well's offer — but on his terms. He goes down with a broadcast rig and opens the phone lines, forcing the entity to hear the callers' testimony on air while he speaks Aldous's buried confession aloud: names, dates, the trade. The well convulses; the seal demands a Vane. Emotional beat: defiant clarity; truth spoken as both weapon and payment.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: POV alternating Sebastian and Ruth. Sebastian gives himself to the well as the children rise out of the floodwater and go home. Ruth keeps the station running, reading his final note on air. Weeks later, a listener calls in just to talk, and a familiar voice answers — gentle, patient, counting the doors between them. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into vigil; belonging found in the darkest frequency.
